--- title: 'NN II -- Compute Graph, Backprop and Training' jupyter: python3 --- ## Introduction [![](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/tools4ds/DS701-Course-Notes/blob/main/ds701_book/jupyter_notebooks/24-NN-II-Backprop.ipynb) In this lecture we'll gradually build out a light weight neural network training framework reminiscent of PyTorch. We build: * A simple neural network engine we call `Value` class that wraps numbers and math operators and includes useful attributes and methods for implementing _forward pass_ and _back propagation_. _(~63 lines of code)_ ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Introduction ::: We'll provide (and explain) * A simple _compute graph_ visualization function. _(34 lines of code)_ * A small set of helper functions that easily define a neuron, layer and multi-layer perceptron (MLP). _(84 lines of code)_ With that we can implement a neural network training loop, and see how similar it is to a PyTorch implementation. The code is based on Andrej Karpathy's [micrograd](https://github.com/karpathy/micrograd). # Artificial Neuron ## Artificial Neuron Recall we looked at an artificial neuron in the [Neural Networks I](23-NN-I-Gradient-Descent.qmd) lecture. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](figs/NN-figs/neuron_model.jpeg){width="100%" .lightbox} From [cs231n](https://cs231n.github.io/neural-networks-1/) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} The common artifical neuron * collects one or more inputs, * each multiplied by a unique weight * sums the weighted inputs * adds a bias * then applies a nonlinear activation function ::: :::: ## Activation Functions The activation function is typically some nonlinear function that compresses the input in some way. Historically, it's been the sigmoid and $\tanh()$ functions.

::: {.callout-important} Without a nonlinear activation function, a neural network collapses to just a linear model and loses all its expressive power. To dive deeper, see the Universal Approximation Theorem in Chapter 3 of [Understanding Deep Learning](https://udlbook.github.io). ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Activation Functions ::: The **sigmoid function** is $$ \mathrm{sigmoid}(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}. $$ ::: {#d5a3306b .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=514 height=376 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Activation Functions ::: The hyperbolic tangent, $\tanh$, is basically the sigmoid function shifted and scaled to a range of [-1,1]. The **tanh** function is $$ \tanh(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}. $$ ::: {#9093d396 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=534 height=376 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Activation Functions ::: A more common activation function these days and that is more efficient to implement is the _Rectified Linear Unit_ or **ReLU**. $$ \textrm{ReLU}(x) = \mathrm{max}(0, x) $$ ::: {#7dff616c .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=427 height=302 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: There are many other variations. See for example [PyTorch Non-linear Activations](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/nn.html#non-linear-activations-weighted-sum-nonlinearity). ## Relating Back to an Earlier Lecture __Question__ What does $$ \mathrm{sigmoid}\left(\sum_i w_i x_i + b\right) \hspace{10pt} \textrm{where} \hspace{10pt} \mathrm{sigmoid}(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} $$ remind you of? :::: {.fragment} __Answer__ How about the Logistic Regression model? In fact, just like in Logistic Regression, we use the sigmoid function on the last layer of a neural network that is doing binary classification to output the probabilities. > So Logistic Regression is similar to one neuron with a sigmoid activation > function. :::: # Fully Connected Network (FCN) ## Fully Connected Network (FCN) ![FCN from UDL.](figs/NN-figs/L24-fcn-dag.png){width="75%" fig-align="center"} * **Layer**: Multiple artificial neurons acting on the same inputs. * **Network**: Multiple cascading __layers__ produce one or more outputs. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Fully Connected Network (FCN) ![FCN from UDL.](figs/NN-figs/L24-fcn-dag.png){width="75%" fig-align="center"} ::: The above network has * _3 inputs_, * three hidden layers of 4, 2 and 3 neurons, respectively, followed by * one layer that produces two continuous value outputs. > This is a **regression model** that is predicting two continuous valued > outputs. ## FCN Matrix Equations We can express the matrix equations for a $K$ layer network as $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_1 &= \mathbf{a}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_0 + \boldsymbol{\Omega}_0 \mathbf{x}) \\ \mathbf{h}_2 &= \mathbf{a}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Omega}_1 \mathbf{h}_1) \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{h}_K &= \mathbf{a}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{K-1} + \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{K-1} \mathbf{h}_{K-1}) \\ \mathbf{\hat{y}} &= \boldsymbol{\beta}_K + \boldsymbol{\Omega}_K \mathbf{h}_K \\ \end{aligned} $$ where $\mathbf{a}(\cdot)$ is the element-wise activation function. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## FCN Matrix Equations ::: The square loss function is $$ L = \sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i = \sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{\hat{y}}_i\|_2^2. $$ The total loss is the sum of the losses over the $i$ training examples. What we want to do is find weights in the NN that minimize the above loss function. We do this by * finding the partial derivatives of $L$ with respect to each parameter in the network * updating the parameters with the negative of its partial derivatives ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## FCN Matrix Equations ::: In other words, we compute $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}_k}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Omega}_k}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}_{k-1}}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{k-1}}, \ldots, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}_0}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Omega}_0}. $$ In the notation above, $\boldsymbol{\beta}_k$ and $\mathbf{\Omega}_k$ are the bias vectors and weight matrices of the $k$-th layer. Just as with partial derivatives with respect to scalars, there are well-defined rules for how to compute the partial derivatives of vector and matrix expressions. PyTorch and TensorFlow implement these calculations. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## FCN Matrix Equations ::: The update rules for the parameters are given by $$ \boldsymbol{\beta}_k \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\beta}_k - \eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}_k}, $$ $$ \boldsymbol{\Omega}_k \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\Omega}_k - \eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Omega}_k}, $$ where $\eta$ is the learning rate. # Computation Graph ## Computation Graph The way we are going to differentiate more complex functions is to first build a "computation graph." We'll see that we can "propagate backwards" through the graph to calculate the gradients of the loss function with respect to the parameters. It's a scalable approach employed by TensorFlow and PyTorch, and in fact we'll follow PyTorch interface definition. ## Building the `Value` Class To do that we will * build a data wrapper as a `class` called `Value`, * gradually build in on all the functionality we need to define a Multi-Layer Neural Network (a.k.a. Multi-Layer Perceptron), * and train the full network. This is similar to how PyTorch defines its `Tensor` class. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Building the `Value` Class ::: First, the class has only a simple initialization method and a representation method. Which we can instantiate and evaluate as follows. ::: {#30aa7486 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` Value(data=4.0) ``` ::: ::: If you are not familiar with [python classes](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/classes.html), there are a few things to note here. 1. The property `self` is just a pointer to the object itself. 2. The `__init__` method is called when you initialize a class object. 3. The `__repr__` method is how you represent the class object. ## Implementing Addition The `Value` object doesn't do much yet except for taking a value and printing it. We'd also like to do things like addition and other operations with them, but... ::: {#b4fe44c7 .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Uh oh! unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Value' and 'Value' ``` ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Implementing Addition ::: When python tries to add two objects `a` and `b`, internally it will call `a.__add__(b)`. We have to add the `__add__()` method. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Implementing Addition ::: Now we try adding two `Value` objects again. ::: {#687d5c69 .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` It worked! ``` ::: ::: Which, as mentioned is equivalent to calling the `__add__` method on `a`. ::: {#4d866ee2 .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` Value(data=1.0) ``` ::: ::: ## Implementing More Operations Similarly we can add define a multiplication operation and a ReLU function. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Implementing More Operations ::: Now we can use the additional operations. ::: {#a3d2b297 .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` Value(data=-4.0) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#6544e7d0 .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` Value(data=0.0) ``` ::: ::: Internally, python will call `__mul__` on `a`, then `__add__` on the temporary product object. ::: {#f77265c7 .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` Value(data=-4.0) ``` ::: ::: ## Child Nodes In order to calculate the gradients, we will need to capture the computation graphs. To do that, we'll need to store pointers to the operands of each operation as a tuple of child nodes in the initializer. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Child Nodes ::: Let's instantiate a few `Value` objects and perform some operations with them. We can now see the children of the operands that produced the output value by printing the `_prev` value. The name `_prev` might not be intuitive yet, but it will make more sense when we view these operations as a graph. ::: {#b639af67 .cell execution_count=17} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` {Value(data=-3.0), Value(data=4.0)} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#f03002f5 .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` {Value(data=-12.0), Value(data=8.0)} ``` ::: ::: ## Child Operations Now we've recorded pointers to the child nodes. It would be helpful to also record the operator used. We'll also add labels for convenience. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Child Operations ::: Let's again instantiate a few `Value` objects and do some operations with them. We can now inspect the parent operands and the operations used to create the current node value. ::: {#fdb2304f .cell execution_count=21} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` ({Value(data=-3.0), Value(data=4.0)}, '*', 'd') ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4ec00b9f .cell execution_count=22} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` ({Value(data=-12.0), Value(data=8.0)}, '+', 'e') ``` ::: ::: ## The Compute Graph We now have enough information stored about the compute graph to visualize it. These are two functions to walk the graph and build sets of all nodes and edges (`trace`) and then draw them as a directed graph (`draw_dot`). ::: {#503008b6 .cell execution_count=24} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-25-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: Note that every value object becomes a node in the graph. The operators are also represented as a kind of fake node so they can be visualized too. ::: {#07bd1ad1 .cell execution_count=25} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Nodes: {Value(data=8.0), Value(data=4.0), Value(data=-3.0), Value(data=-12.0), Value(data=-4.0)} Edges: {(Value(data=-12.0), Value(data=-4.0)), (Value(data=-3.0), Value(data=-12.0)), (Value(data=4.0), Value(data=-12.0)), (Value(data=8.0), Value(data=-4.0))} ``` ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## The Compute Graph ::: Lets add one more operation, or stage, in the compute graph. ::: {#582178de .cell execution_count=26} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-27-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ## Recap So far we've: * built a `Value` class and associated data structures, * captured a computational graph, and * calculated the output based on the inputs and operations. We'll call this the __forward pass__ (or forward propagation). We now need to calculate the gradient of the loss function $L$ with respect to the parameters of the model. Next we'll update our `Value` class to capture the partial derivative at each node relative to `L`. # Calculating Gradients ## Calculating Gradients We now add a gradient member variable, `grad`, to our class to store the partial derivative of the node with respect to the output node. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Calculating Gradients ::: We update `draw_dot()` to show `grad` in the node info. We also reinitialize and redraw the computational graph. ::: {#e8db512a .cell execution_count=29} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-30-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: We have placeholders for the gradients, but they are currently all zero. ## Manual Gradient Calculation Before we start implementing backpropagation, it is helpful to manually calculate some gradients to better understand the procedure. For the node $L$, we trivially calculate $\frac{dL}{dL} = 1$. We can easily see this from the limit ratio perspective, $$ \frac{dL}{dL} = \lim_{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{ (L+h) - L }{h} = \frac{h}{h} = 1 $$ Let's set the gradient of the last node `L` to 1. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Manual Gradient Calculation ::: If we go backwards a step in the graph, we see that $L=e*f$, so we calculate $$ \frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{e}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial{e}} (e\times f) = f, $$ and $$ \frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{f}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial{f}} (e\times f) = e. $$ So we just assign the gradient value to the value of the other operand node. ::: {.callout-tip} For **products**, the partial derivative w.r.t. to one operand is simply the _other operand_. ::: ::: {.callout-important} We needed the node values, e.g., `e.data` and `f.data`, in order to update the gradients. Remember, we calculate all the node values in the **forward pass**. ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Manual Gradient Calculation ::: We again redraw the above computational graph . ::: {#6cc72360 .cell execution_count=32} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-33-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Manual Gradient Calculation ::: How do the parameters $e$ and $f$ influence $L$? Here's a function to vary (or wiggle) them and see the effect on $L$. Let's invoke it with no change $0$ and then a change of $1$. ::: {#f8331824 .cell execution_count=34} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Value(data=-8.0) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#aa1f2636 .cell execution_count=35} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Value(data=-12.0) ``` ::: ::: __Question__ What does $L$ change by if we change $f$ by 1? How much would $L$ change if we changed $e$ by 1? Comment line 12 and uncomment line 10 to check your answer. ## Propagating Back ::: {#b666238d .cell execution_count=36} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=36} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-37-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: Now we want to calculate $$ \frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{c}}, $$ i.e., we want to know how much $L$ varies if we vary $c$, or how $c$ influences $L$. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Propagating Back ::: {#917cd7f7 .cell execution_count=37} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=37} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-38-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: Looking at the graph again we see that $c$ influences $e$ and $e$ influences $L$, so we should be able see the ripple effect of $c$ on $L$. $$ c \rightarrow e \rightarrow L. $$ ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Propagating Back ::: {#2e7218b5 .cell execution_count=38} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=38} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-39-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: We have that $e = c + d$, and so we calculate $$ \frac{\partial{e}}{\partial{c}} = \frac{\partial{}}{\partial{c}} (d + c) = 1. $$ ::: {.callout-tip} For **addition**, the partial derivative w.r.t. to one operand is 1. ::: ## Question $$ c \rightarrow e \rightarrow L $$ Now we know $\partial{L}/\partial{e}$ and we also know $\partial{e}/\partial{c}$, How do we get $\partial{L}/\partial{c}$? ## The Chain Rule To paraphrase from the Wikipedia page on [Chain rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_rule), if a variable $L$ depends on the variable $e$, which itself depends on the variable $c$, then $L$ depends on $c$ as well, via the intermediate variable $e$. In this case, the chain rule is expressed as $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial e} \cdot \frac{\partial e}{\partial c}, $$ and $$ \left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}\right|_{c} = \left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial e}\right|_{e(c)}\cdot \left. \frac{\partial e}{\partial c}\right|_{c}. $$ The above notation indicates at which points the derivatives have to be evaluated. > We evaluate the derivatives at the specific values of the variables that we > calculated in the forward pass. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## The Chain Rule ::: Since we've established that $$ \frac{\partial{e}}{\partial{c}} = 1, $$ then $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial e} \cdot \frac{\partial{e}}{\partial{c}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial e} \cdot 1. $$ In the case of an operand in an addition operation, we just copy the gradient of the parent node. Or put another way: ::: {.callout-important} With the **addition operator**, we just _route the parent gradient to the child_. ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## The Chain Rule ::: So let's assign the gradient of `e` to `d` and `c`. And redraw the graph. ::: {#48e53931 .cell execution_count=40} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=40} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-41-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## The Chain Rule ::: How does $c$ and $d$ influence $L$? Let's look at the effect `c` has on `L`. ::: {#9587e44b .cell execution_count=42} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Value(data=-8.0) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#087208b5 .cell execution_count=43} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Value(data=-6.0) ``` ::: ::: Change the code to see the effect of `d` on `L`. ## Propagating Back Again ::: {#3bdd8027 .cell execution_count=44} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=44} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-45-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: Now we want to calculate $\frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{b}}$ and $\frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{a}}$ but we have $\frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{d}}$ and we know that $$ \frac{\partial{d}}{\partial{b}} = \frac{\partial{}}{\partial{b}}(a\cdot b) = a, $$ so again from the chain rule $$ \frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{b}} = \frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{d}} \cdot \frac{\partial{d}}{\partial{b}} = \frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{d}} \cdot a. $$ ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Propagating Back Again ::: {#de473d99 .cell execution_count=45} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=45} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-46-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: If we expanded all the partial derivatives, we would get $$ \frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{b}} = \left(\frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{e}} \cdot \frac{\partial{e}}{\partial{d}}\right) \cdot \frac{\partial{d}}{\partial{b}}. $$ ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Propagating Back Again ::: Let's assign the gradient values to `b` and `a`. ::: {#9247826a .cell execution_count=46} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=46} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-47-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: We've traversed all the way back to the inputs and calculated all the partial derivatives. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Propagating Back Again ::: Now we can see the effects of varying `b` and `a`. Let's look at the effect `b` has on `L` if we wiggle it by 0 and 1. ::: {#28836985 .cell execution_count=48} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Value(data=-8.0) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#ab3261ef .cell execution_count=49} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Value(data=0.0) ``` ::: ::: Change the code to see the effect of `a` on `L`. ## Recap As you saw, we recursively went backwards through the computation graph and applied the local gradients to the gradients calculated so far to get the partial gradients. > We propagated this calculation backwards through the graph. Of course, in practice, we will only need the gradients on the parameters, not the inputs, so we won't bother calculating them on inputs. ::: {.callout-note} PyTorch let's you control this by setting the `requires_grad` flag on Tensors. ::: _This is the essence of Back Propagation._ # Model Optimization ## A Step in Optimization Let's take a look at the graph again. ::: {#0553a0bc .cell execution_count=50} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=50} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-51-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: Assume we want the value of L to _decrease_. We are free to change the values of the leaf nodes -- all the other nodes are derived from children and leaf nodes. The leaf nodes are $a, b, c$ and $f$. > In practice only update the parameter leaf nodes, not the input > leaf node, but we'll ignore that distinction temporarily for this example. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## A Step in Optimization ::: Let's check the current value of L. ::: {#7314087c .cell execution_count=51} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` -8.0 ``` ::: ::: As we showed before, we want to nudge each of those leaf nodes by the negative of the gradient, multiplied by a step size, $\eta$, i.e., $$ w_{n+1} = w_n - \eta * \frac{\partial{L}}{\partial{w_n}}, $$ where $n$ is the step number. ::: {#8ffad424 .cell execution_count=52} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` -9.230591999999998 ``` ::: ::: Observe that the value of L has indeed decreased. ## A Single Neuron Let's programmatically define a single neuron with * two inputs * two weights (1 for each input) * a bias * the ReLU activation function Recall the neuron figure above. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## A Single Neuron ::: We can draw this compute graph: ::: {#16aa8017 .cell execution_count=54} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=54} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-55-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## A Single Neuron ::: The only new operation we've added is the ReLU, so let's take a quick look at how we differentiate the ReLU. Like before, for the output node, o: $$ \frac{\partial o}{\partial o} = 1. $$ ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## A Single Neuron ::: ReLU is technically not differentiable at 0, but practically we implement the derivative as 0 when $\le 0$ and 1 when $1 > 0$ ![](figs/NN-figs/Train2ReLUDeriv.svg){width="50%" fig-align="center"} ## Coding Backpropagation We'll update our `Value` class once more to support the backward pass. There's a * private `_backward()` function _in each operator_ that implements the local step of the chain rule, and * a `backward()` function in the class that topologically sorts the graph and calls the operator `_backward()` function starting at the end of the graph and going _backward_. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Coding Backpropagation ::: We redefined the class so we have to reinitialize the objects and run the operations again. This constitutes the _forward pass_. ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Coding Backpropagation ::: So we've filled the data values for all the nodes, but haven't calculated the gradients. ::: {#f313bb6e .cell execution_count=59} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=59} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-60-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Coding Backpropagation ::: All we have to do is call the `backward()` method of the last node... and voila! We have all the gradients. ::: {#9c5fb4e6 .cell execution_count=61} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=61} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-62-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ## Accumulating the Gradients You might have noticed that we are accumulating the gradients. This is because we calculate the gradient for each sample in a batch and then sum them up to calculate the average gradient for the batch. The risk now is that if you don't zero the gradients for the next iteration, you will have incorrect gradients. ::: {.callout-warning} Always remember to zero the gradient after each iteration where you update the parameters! ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="web"} ## Accumulating the Gradients -- Special Cases There are also special cases to handle such as when a `Value` object is on both sides of the operand like ::: {#2f7c8291 .cell execution_count=62} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=62} ``` Value(data=3.0, grad=2.0) ``` ::: ::: If we didn't have the accumulation, then `a.grad = 1` instead. Or the other case where a node goes to different operations. ::: {#035ebff3 .cell execution_count=63} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=63} ![](24-NN-II-Backprop_files/figure-revealjs/cell-64-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} We can verify that the gradients are correct analytically. To find the partial derivative $\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}$, we first need to define $f$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. Given $$ \begin{aligned} d &= a \times b, \\ e &= a + b, \\ f &= d \times e \end{aligned} $$ then $f$ can be expanded as $$ \begin{aligned} f &= (a \times b) \times (a + b), \\ &= a^2 \times b + a \times b^2. \end{aligned} $$ Next, we find the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $a$ $$ \frac{\partial f}{\partial a} = 2a \times b + b^2. $$ Finally, we plug in the given values $a = -2.0$ and $b = 3.0$ $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial f}{\partial a} &= 2(-2.0) \times 3.0 + 3.0^2, \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial a} &= -12.0 + 9.0 , \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial a} &= -3.0. \end{aligned} $$ So the partial derivative $\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}$ for the value $a = -2.0$ is $-3.0$. ::: ::: ## Enhancements to `Value` Class There are still some useful operations that `Value` doesn't support, so to be more complete we have the final version of the `Value` class below. We added: * `__radd__` for when the `Value` object is the right operand of an add * `__rmul__` for when the `Value` object is the right operand of a product * `__pow__` to support the ** operator * plus some others you can see below ## Comparing to PyTorch We're using a class implementation that resembles the PyTorch implementation, and in fact we can compare our implementation with PyTorch. ::: {#b70dab2e .cell execution_count=66} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.881373405456543 --- x2.grad 1.0 w2.grad 0.0 x1.grad -3.0 w1.grad 2.0 ``` ::: ::: By default, tensors don't store gradients and so won't support backprop, so we explicitly set `requires_grad = True`. # Building a Neural Network ## Neural Network Modules Now we'll define some classes which help us build out a small neural network. __Module__ -- A base class __Neuron__ -- Implement a single linear or nonlinear neuron with `nin` inputs. __Layer__ -- Implement a layer of network consisting of `nout` neurons, each taking `nin` inputs __MLP__ -- A _Multi-Layer Perceptron_ that implements `len(nouts)` layers of neurons.
